title: Sentence Foundations: Pepeke Painu
description: Study a source-checked action sentence, compare its negative form, and test whether you can identify the main parts.

sourceReview.notes: Examples and verbal-marker forms are taken from UH Maui College's Pepeke Painu page. New checks ask learners to recognize source-listed structures without inventing additional Hawaiian sentences.

activities.instruction: See how the sentence is built.
activities.prompt: Start with the Hawaiian pattern instead of forcing English word order onto it.
activities.support: Read the whole sentence first, then look at the three parts.
activities.sentence: ʻAi ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.patternIntro: In this sourced example, the action comes first, followed by who is doing it, then what the action is directed toward.

parts.label: Action
parts.note: The sentence begins with the action: eat/eats.

parts.label: Who
parts.note: This identifies Lani as the person doing the action.

parts.label: What
parts.note: This tells what the action is directed toward: the poi.

activities.languageNote: For now, notice the shape: Action → Who → What. The Hawaiian sentence does not need to copy English word order.

activities.instruction: Identify the part of the sentence.
activities.prompt: ʻAi ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.support: Which part tells you who is doing the action?
activities.explanation: In this example, ʻo Lani identifies Lani as the person doing the action.

activities.instruction: Identify the part of the sentence.
activities.prompt: ʻAi ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.support: Which part tells what Lani eats?
activities.explanation: In this example, i ka poi identifies what the action is directed toward.

activities.instruction: Identify the part of the sentence.
activities.prompt: ʻAi ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.explanation: ʻAi is the action at the beginning of this example.

activities.instruction: Compare the positive and negative forms.
activities.prompt: Look at what changes when the sourced example is made negative.
activities.support: Read the negative sentence as a whole before comparing the parts.
activities.sentence: ʻAʻole ʻai ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.patternIntro: UH Maui College presents this negative form alongside the positive example. Notice ʻAʻole at the beginning before ʻai.

parts.label: Negative
parts.note: The negative form begins with ʻAʻole in this example.

parts.label: Action + Who
parts.note: The action and the person remain visible after the negative opening.

parts.label: What
parts.note: The part referring to poi remains at the end.

activities.languageNote: At this stage, the goal is recognition: see the contrast between the two sourced sentences before trying to generate negative sentences yourself.

activities.prompt: Which sourced sentence says that Lani does not eat poi?
activities.support: Look for the negative opening shown in the previous screen.
options: ʻAi ʻo Lani i ka poi.
ʻAʻole ʻai ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.answer: ʻAʻole ʻai ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.explanation: The negative example begins with ʻAʻole: ʻAʻole ʻai ʻo Lani i ka poi.

activities.prompt: ʻAi ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.support: Which order best describes the three parts you studied?
activities.explanation: For this sourced example, the lesson breaks the sentence into Action → Who → What.

activities.prompt: Which sourced example begins with the Ua PAINU pattern?
activities.support: UH Maui College lists Ua PAINU among the Pepeke Painu verbal markers.
options: Ua hoʻi mai nei ke koa i Hawaiʻi
ʻApōpō, e hiki mai ana ka mokulele i ka hola ʻumi.
ʻAi ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.answer: Ua hoʻi mai nei ke koa i Hawaiʻi
activities.explanation: UH Maui College gives “Ua hoʻi mai nei ke koa i Hawaiʻi” as an example under the Pepeke Painu verbal-marker section.

activities.prompt: Which sourced example shows an e ... ana pattern?
activities.support: Look for e before the action and ana after it.
options: Ua hoʻi mai nei ke koa i Hawaiʻi
ʻApōpō, e hiki mai ana ka mokulele i ka hola ʻumi.
ʻAi ʻo Lani i ka poi.
activities.answer: ʻApōpō, e hiki mai ana ka mokulele i ka hola ʻumi.
activities.explanation: In the UH Maui College example, e comes before hiki and ana follows it: e hiki mai ana.

activities.instruction: Identify the marker around the action.
activities.prompt: ʻApōpō, e hiki mai ana ka mokulele i ka hola ʻumi.
activities.support: Which pair surrounds the action hiki in this sourced example?
activities.explanation: The example contains e hiki mai ana, so the visible marker pair is e ... ana.
